query: In the object parser's JIT fastpass, the branch handling an optional key returns early instead of running the assignment. What concrete bug did that early return fix?
In the object parser's JIT fastpass, the branch handling an optional key returns early instead of running the assignment. What concrete bug did that early return fix?
text:
fix(v4): align object and tuple optionality handling (#5661) fix(v4): align object and tuple optionality handling (#5661)

* fix(v4): apply trailing tuple defaults via optout flag

Tuple elements with `.default()` / `.prefault()` were silently dropped
when the input array was shorter than the tuple, because the parser
skipped any item past `input.length` whose slot was within `optStart`.

Gate the skip on `optout === "optional"` instead. That distinguishes
schemas that produce `undefined` for missing input (`.optional()`,
`z.undefined()`) — for which skipping is a no-op — from schemas that
produce a defined value. `optout` already bubbles through `nullable` /
`readonly` / `catch` / `pipe` / `union`, so chains like
`.default("x").nullable()` are covered without a type-name allowlist.

Closes #5229.

* test(v4): match tuple `_input` shape under tsc latest

`expectTypeOf<...>().toEqualTypeOf<[string, string?]>()` rejects the
inferred `[string, (string | undefined)?]` under TypeScript >=6 because
the optional element widens to `T | undefined` in the source position.

* fix(v4): keep tuple result dense when an optional precedes a default

The previous fix for #5229 left a sparse hole when an `.optional()`
slot sat between the input boundary and a later `.default()` — e.g.
`tuple([s, s.optional(), s.default("z")]).parse(["a"])` produced
`["a", <empty>, "z"]`, which fails `1 in r`, JSON-serializes to
`null`, and skips iteration.

Walk trailing items from the end to find the highest index whose
schema fills missing input (`optout !== "optional"`). Run every slot
up to that point so `.optional()` items reached while padding for a
later default produce explicit `undefined`. When the tail is purely
optional, the length-shortening behavior is preserved.

* refactor(v4): mirror $ZodObject in $ZodTuple parser

Drop the bespoke `runUntil` reverse-find scan in favor of the same
shape used by `$ZodObject`: run every item with `value: input[i]`
(undefined past the input boundary), let each schema decide what
undefined means, and have `handleTupleResult` swallow errors from
absent optional-out slots — the tuple-index analog of
`handlePropertyResult`'s `key in input` check.

A small post-loop trim drops trailing slots that produced `undefined`
for absent input (preserves the existing length-shortening behaviour
for purely-optional tails like `[s, s.optional()] / [a]`).

Behaviour identical to the previous fix on every case in the suite,
but the parser now reads alongside the object parser instead of
introducing a second, structurally-identical reverse-find boundary.

* fix(v4): break tuple parsing on first absent-optional rejection

When a tuple slot past `optStart` rejects `undefined` (e.g. an
`.optional()` chain with a refine that bans `undefined`), swallow the
issue and truncate the result there. Critically, also stop processing
later items so subsequent `.default()` slots do NOT materialize on top
of an already-malformed tail.

Previously the parser swallowed the absent-optional error but kept
running, letting a later default produce a value at an index past the
"missing" slot and yielding e.g. `["alpha", undefined, "d"]` for input
`["alpha"]`. Now the result is `["alpha"]`, matching the array-analog
of $ZodObject's absent-optional-key behaviour.

Implementation: parse all items in parallel, collect into an indexed
results array, then iterate in order during finalize — break on the
first absent-optional rejection, then run the trailing-undefined trim
so optional slots between the last real input and the rejected slot
also collapse away.

* test(v4): cover multi-trailing optional tuple cases

Lock in that:
- multiple trailing `.optional()` elements still trim back to the input
  length (we don't fill the tail with literal `undefined`s)
- explicit `undefined` inside `input.length` IS preserved
- trailing optionals after a default that fires are still trimmed

* refactor(v4): hoist tuple finalize into top-level handleTupleResults

The post-processing for tuple parse results (in-order walk with
break-on-absent-optional-error, then trailing-undefined trim) was
defined as a closure inside the parse hot path. Hoist it to a
top-level `handleTupleResults` helper, mirroring the `handle*Result`
convention already used for objects and rest items.

Also document why `optStart` is intentionally NOT consulted in
finalize: it's an input-length concern handled by the `too_small`
precheck at the top of parse. Output shaping uses `optout` instead so
that a `.default()` tail item — which sits inside the optStart region
but materializes a defined value — is correctly preserved rather than
dropped or swallowed.

Adds a regression test that explicit `undefined` inside the input is
preserved even when the element schema produces `undefined` as a
valid output (e.g. `z.string().or(z.undefined())`,
`z.string().optional()`, `z.undefined()`). The trim's
\`i >= input.length\` floor is what guards this.

* fix: drop `z.undefined()`'s `optout = "optional"`

Bundled into #4769 alongside the legitimate `optin = "optional"` fix
for #4768 without separate justification. The test added in the same
commit literally has `// z.undefined should NOT be optional` directly
above an assertion saying it is.

`optout` is read by the object parser's absent-key error-swallow path
(#5589) and the tuple parser's `optStart`. Marking `z.undefined()`
optout-optional conflates "value type is undefined" with "key may be
absent in inferred output," which is upstream of the confusion in
#5654 and #5661.

Inference doesn't move: `\$ZodUndefinedInternals` doesn't promote
`optin`/`optout` to required fields, so `z.object({ a: z.undefined() })`
already infers as `{ a: undefined }` regardless. `optin = "optional"`
stays — that one is the JSON-schema `required`-array fix from #4768.

* fix: drop `z.undefined()`'s `optin = "optional"` too

Same conflation as the previous commit, on the input side. The motivating
JSON-schema bug from #4768 is `.catch()`-specific; the analogous extension
to `z.undefined()` was opportunistic. Under strict semantics
`z.object({ a: z.undefined() })` infers as `{ a: undefined }` (required
key) and the JSON-schema `required` array should agree. Runtime stays
permissive — `z.undefined().parse(undefined)` succeeds whether the source
was an absent key or an explicit `undefined`.

* test(v4): adapt tuple tests to z.undefined()'s required-input semantics

After dropping z.undefined()'s `optin`/`optout = "optional"` flags, a
trailing `z.undefined()` slot is required input — omitting it triggers
`too_small` rather than trimming. Update the assertions accordingly,
and lock in the error shape with inline snapshots since the precheck
abort behaviour (single `too_small`, no element-level errors) is the
exact piece worth pinning.

Also tighten the "required slot fails past input length" test to
snapshot the issue list instead of just `success === false`, so the
shape — single `too_small` from the precheck rather than e.g. an
`invalid_type` from the per-item run — is unambiguous.

* fix(v4): reject absent object keys when optin is required

Object parsing should only treat key absence as acceptable when the input-side optionality flag says so. Keep optout for output shaping, but stop letting schemas that merely accept or catch undefined make a required key disappear.

query: In the object parser's JIT fastpass, the branch handling an optional key returns early instead of running the assignment. What concrete bug did that early return fix?
text:
fix(v4): an absent key on the middle rung supplies nothing (#6434) fix(v4): an absent key on the middle rung supplies nothing (#6434)

* fix(v4): an absent key on the middle rung supplies nothing

The optin ladder defines "optional" as "the container may omit it;
nothing is supplied in its place". An absent key whose schema declares
that rung was still assigned whatever the schema made of `undefined`,
so `z.object({ a: z.coerce.string().exactOptional() }).parse({})`
returned `{ a: "undefined" }`.

Gate on the ladder at the one place that knows presence. `catch` and
`preprocess` are optional-in only, so they keep filling absent keys;
`default` and `prefault` sit on the top rung and still substitute.
All three parse paths get the gate, or compile mode diverges.

* refactor: pass optout raw alongside optin

Both optionality axes now arrive at handlePropertyResult as the raw
structural property rather than one enum and one pre-computed boolean.

* test: pin absent keys with toStrictEqual, and reunite a comment with its function

toEqual treats { a: undefined } as equal to {}, so the assertions pinned
that the invented value was gone but not that the key was — the exact
distinction this change establishes. dropsWhenAbsent had also landed
between mayOutputUndefined's comment and mayOutputUndefined itself.

query: Why does the closed-key pass-through in record parsing explicitly skip the key __proto__?
text:
fix: honor loose mode for closed record key schemas (#6157) fix: honor loose mode for closed record key schemas (#6157)

* fix: honor loose mode for closed record key schemas

* fix(record): don't pass __proto__ through looseRecord's closed key path

The closed-key pass-through added here writes into a plain {} from a
for...in loop, so an own "__proto__" key (JSON.parse produces one)
replaced the result's prototype. The open-key branch and z.object's
catchall loop already skip it; mirror that.

query: Why does the closed-key pass-through in record parsing explicitly skip the key __proto__?
text:
fix(v4): re-check the record key after the key schema runs (#6355) fix(v4): re-check the record key after the key schema runs (#6355)

The record parser skips an input key when the raw key is exactly
__proto__, but it writes the parsed value under the key the key schema
produced. A key schema that normalizes keys therefore walks straight
past the guard: z.record(z.string().toLowerCase(), ...) parsing
{"__PROTO__": {...}} assigns through the inherited setter and replaces
the prototype of the parsed result with attacker-supplied data.

The guard and the write reason about different keys. Check the key we
actually write under, and drop it there — matching what the raw-key
guard already does, and what v3 did with a single guard on the
post-transform key in mergeObjectSync.

Reaches every key-transform mechanism: toLowerCase, trim, normalize,
transform, overwrite, preprocess, pipe and codec, sync and async, in
both classic and mini. A fullwidth key normalizing under NFKC hits it
too. Declared __proto__ keys are unaffected — those are #6354.

Reported by @joostgrunwald.

text:
fix(v4): report own __proto__ key under .strict() (#6221) fix(v4): report own __proto__ key under .strict() (#6221)

* fix(v4): report own __proto__ key under .strict()

* fix(object): don't report a declared __proto__ field as unrecognized

The __proto__ branch ran before the keySet check, so once #6354 made a
declared __proto__ shape key round-trip, .strict() started rejecting
input the schema explicitly allows. Check keySet first; the shape loop
already owns declared keys, and only an undeclared __proto__ should be
reported.

Also pins strictObject/jitless parity and the declared-key case across
strict, catchall and plain objects.

query: Why does the issue emitted by an exclusive union (z.xor) carry a `matches` array of option indices?
text:
fix(v4): give z.xor() a distinct error when multiple options match (#6376) fix(v4): give z.xor() a distinct error when multiple options match (#6376)

* fix(v4): give z.xor() a distinct error when multiple options match (#6342)

An exclusive union that failed because *several* options matched emitted
`invalid_union` with `errors: []` and `inclusive: false`, and the English
error map had no case for it — so the message was a bare "Invalid input"
with nothing pointing at the overlap.

The issue now carries `matches`, the indices of the options that matched,
and en reports "expected exactly one matching option, received 2
(options 0, 1)". The zero-match path is unchanged and still reports each
option's own errors.

* fix(v4): simplify the xor multi-match message

The message no longer restates the count and indices — `matches` on the
issue is the granular channel, and the docs point at it.

query: Why does the issue emitted by an exclusive union (z.xor) carry a `matches` array of option indices?
text:
fix(v4): infer recursive getter options in discriminatedUnion (#6422) fix(v4): infer recursive getter options in discriminatedUnion (#6422)

* fix(v4): infer recursive getter options in discriminatedUnion

The option bound resolved each option's `input` to check that it carried the
discriminator. That forces TypeScript to evaluate the input while checking the
call, which is circular for an option whose input references the union itself —
so a mutually-recursive getter schema collapsed the whole union to `any` and
emitted ts7022/ts2615, while the equivalent `z.union` inferred fine.

Drop the compile-time discriminator check. The bound now stops at `propValues`
and rests on `SomeType`, matching every other schema generic in the codebase.
A missing or non-literal discriminator is still rejected — by
`$ZodDiscriminatedUnion` when it builds its lookup map, on the first parse,
whatever the input.

Diagnosis from #6013; closes #5991 and #5288.

* test: pin the discriminator branch, and keep $ZodTypeDiscriminable's type param

Two predicates reject a bad option and both throw the same message, but only
the lookup map reads `def.discriminator`. The tests used
`z.object({ value: z.string() })`, which has empty `propValues` and so trips
the emptiness branch — reachable before this PR and not the guarantee it
trades away. Pin the case this PR newly admits: an option with a literal-valued
property that is not the discriminator, which passes `propValues` and fails
when the map is built.

Restore the (unused) type parameter on `$ZodTypeDiscriminable` and
`$ZodTypeDiscriminableInternals` so `$ZodTypeDiscriminable<"kind">` keeps
compiling for external callers, and record in the comment that eager
construction-time validation is unavailable rather than merely unchosen — it
hits a TDZ ReferenceError on exactly the recursive schemas this enables.

* feat(v4): check the discriminator at construction via propKeys

Adds `propKeys` to the object def: the schema's own property names, built with
`Object.keys` so it never invokes the shape's getters. `$ZodDiscriminatedUnion`
checks its discriminator against each option's `propKeys` when it is
constructed, so an object option that forgot the key fails at the
`z.discriminatedUnion()` call rather than on the first object parsed.

Reading `def.shape` instead would work for plain schemas but spreads the shape,
running every getter, which is a TDZ ReferenceError for the mutually-recursive
options this bound exists to support. `Object.keys` avoids that entirely.

Placement is deliberate: on `def`, not `_zod`. An object's `def` is already a
dictionary-mode object, so an extra entry costs ~72 B on a 3-key schema, where
a `util.defineLazy` property on `_zod` cost ~784 B and pushed `_zod` from 11 to
12 own properties. `_zod` is unchanged.

`mergeDefs` copies non-enumerable descriptors, so a derived def would otherwise
inherit the source's list and reject a discriminator the derived schema does
have. Defs whose shape is a getter (`.extend()`, `.merge()`) clear it instead
and fall back to the lookup-map check, as do options with no `propKeys` at all
(pipes, lazies, wrappers).

Measured against be1468b8 on an idle machine, interleaved, one case per
process: memory +32 B empty / +72 B 3-key / +128 B 10-key per object schema and
0 B for non-objects; bundle +17 B gz classic, +27 B gz mini; `z.object()`
construction +1.4%; discriminated-union parse unchanged.

* fix(v4): correct the propKeys comments and guard a shapeless def

The `core/api.ts` comment still claimed eager validation was unavailable, which
the previous commit made false — only the `propValues` route is blocked, and
`propKeys` works precisely because `Object.keys` does not invoke getters.

Name what actually loses the key list. Every builder that rebuilds the def gives
it a getter-backed shape — `.extend()`, `.omit()`, `.pick()`, `.partial()`,
`.describe()`, `.meta()`, `.check()` — so the construction-time check covers
freshly built objects only, not derived ones.

`Object.keys(sh)` threw for a def with no shape where the previous spread
tolerated it; only reachable through the exported `$ZodObject`, but it was a new
eager crash on a public export.

* fix(v4): make propKeys an accessor, and strip it in mergeDefs

Two defects, one root cause.

Deriving a schema mutated the schema it was derived from. `.describe()`,
`.meta()` and `.clone()` reuse the def by identity, so the object constructor
ran again on the same def, took the getter-shape branch, and wrote
`propKeys: undefined` over a list that was correct — silently disabling the
construction-time check for the receiver.

The eager snapshot also disagreed with the shape it described. `shape` resolves
lazily from the object the caller passed, so mutating that object after
construction left `propKeys` stale and made `discriminatedUnion` reject an
option that does carry the discriminator, in a program that works on main.

`propKeys` is now an accessor over the captured shape, so it always answers for
the current shape, and `mergeDefs` strips it so a genuinely new def cannot
inherit the source's. The defensive else branch — the cause of the first defect
and of the `.extend()` construction regression — is gone.

Def-sharing builders therefore keep their list, so the check now also covers
`.describe()`, `.meta()`, `.brand()`, `.clone()`, `.catchall()`, `.strict()`
and `.loose()`. It still does not cover the builders that change the property
set (`.extend()`, `.omit()`, `.pick()`, `.partial()`, `.check()`,
`.readonly()`), whose shape cannot be enumerated without resolving it.

* Revert "feat(v4): check the discriminator at construction via propKeys"

Reverts 36eff8ef, 0159ecb0 and 68cbe754, restoring the type-only fix.

The construction-time check cost more than it was worth on every axis, and each
attempt to make it correct opened a new hole:

- the first version cleared `propKeys` on defs it did not own, so `.describe()`
  silently disabled the check for the schema it was called on;
- the accessor that fixed that froze at a different moment than `def.shape`
  does, so deleting a shape key after the first read made `discriminatedUnion`
  reject an option that does carry the discriminator — a false rejection, in a
  program that works on main.

Measured against the type-only baseline, the accessor form costs +480 B per
object schema (+7% to +11%), flat regardless of key count, because it pays an
AccessorPair and a closure where the snapshot paid a key array. That is a
universal cost on every object schema in every program, and it bought a
diagnostic that never covered `.extend()`, `.omit()`, `.pick()`, `.partial()`,
`.check()` or `.readonly()`, whose shapes cannot be enumerated without
resolving them.

A malformed discriminated union is caught by the lookup map on first parse, as
it was before this branch.

* docs(v4): scope the "not available" claim to propValues

The revert carried this comment back to its original wording, which says eager
validation at construction is unavailable. That is only true of the `propValues`
route. `Object.keys` lists a shape's keys without invoking them, so an eager
check is reachable — it was tried on this branch and reverted because a derived
key list cannot be kept in agreement with `shape`, which resolves lazily and
then freezes, and because it charged every object schema for a check only
discriminated unions read.

This comment is the only record of that inside the codebase, so it should say
why the door is shut rather than imply there is no door.

* feat(v4): check the discriminator when the union is constructed

A malformed discriminated union was only caught when its lookup map was built,
on the first object parsed — and the parse path reaches that map only after the
input passes `util.isObject`, so `safeParse(123)` left it undiscovered.

`$ZodObject` records the object its `shape` currently answers from, and
`$ZodDiscriminatedUnion` checks its discriminator against that when it is
constructed. `Object.keys` lists a shape's keys without invoking them, which is
what makes this safe for the mutually-recursive getter options this branch
exists to support — reading `propValues` or `def.shape` would run those getters
and throw `ReferenceError: Cannot access '...' before initialization`.

Holding the shape object rather than a key list derived from it is what keeps
the two in agreement. `shape` answers from the caller's object until the first
read and from a frozen copy after it; a list derived at either moment disagrees
at the other, and either way the union rejects options that do carry the
discriminator.

Keyed by def in a module-private WeakMap rather than stored on the def. A def
rebuilt by a builder is a different object and is therefore simply absent,
where a property would be copied by `mergeDefs` and need clearing there —
shared machinery carrying one type's concern. Builders that reuse the def by
identity, such as `.describe()`, keep the check; those that rebuild it, such as
`.extend()`, fall back to the lookup map.

Measured against 4199f248: 0 B retained per schema, +15 B gzipped classic and
+23 B mini, no parse-path change.

* fix(v4): the construction check must use hasOwnProperty, not `in`

`in` walks the prototype chain, so the check silently no-opped whenever the
discriminator was named after an `Object.prototype` member — `toString`,
`constructor`, `valueOf` — while `type` in the same position threw. It also
contradicted the comment above it, which says the keys are read with
`Object.keys`.

* test(treeshake): raise the zod-mini-object ceiling for the construction check

The construction-time discriminator check writes a WeakMap entry from
`$ZodObject`, so every bundle containing `z.object` carries it whether or not it
ever builds a discriminated union. `zod-mini-object` measures 4260 against the
4257 ceiling.

Raised to 4288, keeping the 28 bytes of headroom the other two fixtures have.
Taken knowingly: the cost is ~23 gzipped bytes on mini, ~42 B per retained
object schema in V8's ephemeron table, and ~10% of `z.object()` construction.

query: Why does the issue emitted by an exclusive union (z.xor) carry a `matches` array of option indices?
text:
fix: preserve explicit superRefine issue input (#6053) fix: preserve explicit superRefine issue input (#6053)

`_issue.input ??= payload.value` discarded an explicitly-supplied nullish `input`, so `superRefine` was the one place in Zod that could not emit an issue whose `input` matched the value-at-the-path convention every builtin issue follows. Forwarding a nested parse's issues was worse: an inner `input: undefined` for a missing key got overwritten with the outer payload, which breaks the documented `iss.input === undefined` test for a missing field.

Switching to a presence check preserves an explicit `null` or `undefined` while still backfilling when `input` is omitted. `undefined` is a meaningful value for `input` in a way it isn't for the `code`/`inst`/`continue` defaults alongside it, which is why only this one moves off `??=`.

Costs 26 B raw in classic, 0 B in mini unless `z.superRefine` is imported. No memory change, and the line only runs when an issue is constructed.

query: Why does the domain regex in regexes.ts begin with a lookahead assertion?
text:
fix(v4): enforce RFC 1035 length limits in regexes.domain (#6035) fix(v4): enforce RFC 1035 length limits in regexes.domain (#6035)

Adds the RFC 1035 length limits that `regexes.hostname` already enforced: a 253-character total via a leading lookahead, and a 63-character cap on the TLD label. Non-TLD labels were already capped at 63 by the existing quantifier.

Also syncs the two literal copies of the pattern — the docs callout and the `httpurl` test comment — and pins the 253-character boundary from both sides.

Closes #5965.

query: Why does the domain regex in regexes.ts begin with a lookahead assertion?
text:
fix(v4): let a schema's error map cover its own checks' issues (#6426) fix(v4): let a schema's error map cover its own checks' issues (#6426)

* fix(v4): let a schema's error map cover its own checks' issues

finalizeIssue walks the error maps in decreasing specificity and stops at the
first message. `inst` is whatever raised the issue, so for a check the first
rung is the check's own map -- and the next rung was the parse call. The
owning schema's map had no rung at all, so z.string({ error }).min(5) never
consulted it.

Adds that rung between the two, which is where specificity puts it: less
specific than the check that failed, more specific than the parse call.
Guarded on schema !== inst so a schema that raised its own issue is not asked
twice. iss.schema comes from #6420, which is what made the owning schema
reachable from here at all.

Rewrites test("z.config customError "). It asserted the global map beats a
schema-bound map, which inverts both the documented precedence and the
sibling test directly above it -- it passed only because the schema map was
never called. That assertion came from v3's overrideErrorMap test, where the
v3 map explicitly deferred via ctx.defaultError for non-invalid_type codes;
the v4 port dropped the deferral and kept the assertion. It now uses a plain
z.string(), so it tests the global map, which is what its name says.

Closes #6108.

* review: make the error-map tests leak-proof and fix the docs example

Two rough edges from review.

The tests that install a global customError reset it on their last line, so a
failing assertion above that line leaks the map into every later test in the
file. That is not hypothetical -- reverting the patch to check the new tests
actually fail turned one real failure into four. A file-level afterEach makes
all four call sites leak-proof, so the three per-test resets come out.

The precedence list's schema-level example was z.string("Not a string!"),
which reads as a type-error message. After this change
z.string("Not a string!").min(5) reports it too, so the example now teaches
the wrong lesson. Uses a check-agnostic message and shows both cases.

* docs: annotate the precedence examples with safeParse, not parse

.parse() throws on failure, so `// => "Invalid name"` read as if it were
the return value. The file's own idiom for this annotation is .safeParse().

query: Why is the ISO date regex built through an anchor() helper instead of an inline template literal?
text:
chore: fail on stacked line comments chore: fail on stacked line comments

Lines have no maximum width in this repo — the editor wraps for display — so
a paragraph broken across several `//` lines is just a hard wrap, and hard
wraps break search, diffs and editing. `pnpm check:comments` now fails on
them, with `--fix` to join the offenders. Wired into pre-commit and the CI
lint job.

Biome 1.9.4 has no such rule and no plugin support, so this is a standalone
check. It reads comments through the TypeScript parser rather than by regex,
so `//` inside a string, template literal or regex is never mistaken for one.

The hard part is that the repo had ~2800 stacked comment lines and almost all
of them are commented-out code, which cannot be joined. The check therefore
separates prose from code and judges each block as a whole: unless every line
reads as prose, the block is left alone. Classifying line by line lets one
code-ish line split a paragraph, after which `--fix` joins the fragment and
strands its tail. Commented-out code, `@ts-*` and `@__NO_SIDE_EFFECTS__`
pragmas, and bullet lists are exempt; a bare `//` is a paragraph break that
starts a new block, and a wrapped bullet item is still reported.

Also joins the 98 existing prose blocks. Twenty join boundaries were fixed by
hand: six were two separate comments about two different statements and got a
blank line instead, and fourteen needed a sentence break.

query: Why is the ISO date regex built through an anchor() helper instead of an inline template literal?
text:
fix(locales): backfill the mac and Sizable.map gaps, and pin dictionary parity (#6427) fix(locales): backfill the mac and Sizable.map gaps, and pin dictionary parity (#6427)

Three keys had drifted the same way credit_card did in #6424: a feature
shipped en and never backfilled the rest. Sizable.map arrived with #5316
(ZodMap sizing) and was missing from 43 of 60 locales; mac arrived with #5440
(MAC validation) and was missing from 49; Hebrew alone also lacked uuidv4,
uuidv6 and template_literal.

Only some of that is user-visible, and the distinction is worth recording.
A missing FormatDictionary key renders the raw key name, which reads fine for
emoji/nanoid/cuid/cuid2 because en maps those to themselves -- they are left
alone deliberately. mac rendered lowercase "mac" instead of "MAC address". A
missing Sizable.map is worse than either: it drops the unit and the verb, so
German said "erwartet, dass map >=2 ist" where en says "expected map to have
>=2 entries".

Most strings are derived from the file's own vocabulary rather than composed:
mac from that locale's ipv4 with the protocol token swapped, Sizable.map from
that locale's set entry.

Approximations, all deliberate:

- Sizable.map copies set's unit everywhere. en distinguishes "entries" from
  "items"; most locales will not want to. be/hy/ru mirror set's plural forms
  rather than the precise word for entries.
- fi needed its own genitive rather than a copy, since its subject field names
  the container: "kuvauksen". Finnish Map terminology is unsettled and this is
  the weakest string here; "sanakirjan" is the alternative.
- az takes English "MAC address" to match its own untranslated ipv4/ipv6/cidrv4.
- ur spells the acronym letter by letter, matching how that file already
  handles json_string, jwt and cuid.

da, nn, no and sv all have ipv4 meaning "range" rather than "address"
("IPv4-omraade", "IPv4-intervall"), which their own email entries contradict.
Deriving mac from those would have said "MAC range", so all four are written
out instead. The ipv4 strings themselves are left as they are -- that is a
separate change.

The parity test is the point of the commit. It reads the key lists out of
en.ts at test time instead of hardcoding them, so adding a format to en
extends it automatically, and it exempts keys en maps to themselves by
probing whether en falls through. A hand-maintained list would miss the next
drift the way the last four were missed.

query: Why is the ISO date regex built through an anchor() helper instead of an inline template literal?
text:
Tighten cuid() regex and deprecate CUID v1 (#5880) Tighten cuid() regex and deprecate CUID v1 (#5880)

- Change cuid regex from `/^[cC][^\s-]{8,}$/` to `/^[cC][0-9a-z]{6,}$/`
  in v4. Restricts the body to base36 (the actual CUID v1 charset) and
  aligns the length floor with Eric Elliott's documented guidance
  ("starts with c, contains at least 7 chars", paralleldrive/cuid#88).
  Brings the regex stylistically in line with the other ID validators
  (ulid, xid, ksuid, nanoid, cuid2), all of which use allowlist
  character classes.

  The change is backwards-compatible for any real CUID v1 output
  (always lowercase base36) and additionally accepts shorter cuid-shaped
  values that the prior `{8,}` floor incorrectly rejected. It rejects
  the punctuation-shaped false positives reported in #3621 and similar.

- Mark CUID v1 surfaces `@deprecated` (function, chain method, schema
  class, internals, regex export) pointing at z.cuid2(). Per the
  upstream repo, "Deprecated collision-resistant id spec. Insecure
  because it leaks timestamps. Use cuid2 instead."

- Add regression tests asserting that previously-accepted non-base36
  payloads are now rejected. Update one template-literal test that was
  relying on the old {8,} floor.

Zod 3 is in maintenance mode and is intentionally left untouched.

query: Why do schema methods live on the prototype rather than as own properties on each instance, and what got measurably worse as a result?
text:
perf(v4): cut per-schema memory ~90% by moving methods to the prototype (#6318) perf(v4): cut per-schema memory ~90% by moving methods to the prototype (#6318)

Schema instances carried their methods as own properties, which put them past the point where V8 stops using inline slots for property storage. Moving those methods to the prototype — where they materialize per instance on first read — cuts a schema's retained size by roughly 90% and makes construction several times faster.

- `z.string()` 7709 → 816 bytes retained; a 10-key object 83928 → 12171; `zod/mini` `z.string()` 2528 → 593
- a 500-schema API catalogue holds 62.7 MB instead of 198.0 MB
- construction is 45–83% faster; parse throughput is unchanged
- bundle grows by a fixed ~150–200 B gzipped (+1% classic, +5% mini), the one axis that regresses

Detachability is preserved — the getters bind on first access and cache, so `const { parse } = schema` and `arr.map(schema.parse)` still work — and descriptor attributes, enumerability and function-identity aliases were diffed against `main` across every schema type to keep the observable surface intact.

Original work and the core insight by @zirkelc.

query: Why do schema methods live on the prototype rather than as own properties on each instance, and what got measurably worse as a result?
text:
perf(v4): lazy-bind builder methods to shared internal prototype (#5897) perf(v4): lazy-bind builder methods to shared internal prototype (#5897)

* perf(v4): lazy-bind builder methods to shared internal prototype

Builder methods (.optional, .nullable, .array, .pick, etc.) were
allocated as fresh per-instance closures during construction. On a
plain z.string() that's ~50 closures up front, dominated by JSFunction
+ Context bytes, even when the user never calls them.

Move builders onto a hidden prototype layer ($internalProto) inserted
between _.prototype (user-extension space) and the parent. On first
access from any instance, defineLazy allocates fn.bind(this) and
caches it as an own enumerable property; subsequent accesses skip the
getter. Detached usage (const m = schema.optional; m()) keeps working
because m is a bound function with this already resolved.

Parse-family methods (parse, safeParse, encode, etc.) intentionally
stay as eager per-instance closures — they're the hot path AND the
most-detached methods (arr.map(schema.parse)), so paying the
allocation up front is worth the monomorphic call site.

Adds a regression test guarding detached method behavior.

* refactor(v4): collapse lazy-bind to a classic-only helper

Two simplifications on top of the previous commit, no behavior change:

1. Remove all changes from `core/core.ts`. The `$internalProto` symbol
   and `defineLazy` helper are gone. Classic now creates the
   library-owned prototype layer lazily on first install per
   constructor, via `Object.setPrototypeOf(constr.prototype, layer)`
   cached in a `WeakMap`. Net diff to `core/core.ts` is zero.

2. Drop all ~50 `_sharedXxx` named functions in favor of inline
   method-shorthand bodies inside each `_installLazyMethods({...})`
   call site. The `_shared` prefix is gone; the only underscore-
   prefixed helper left in classic is `_installLazyMethods` itself.

Bundle size impact (esbuild --bundle --minify --format=esm, gzipped):

  Classic minimal (z.string().parse): 15,677 -> 15,889 (+212 B, +1.4%)
  Classic rich (object schema):       19,100 -> 19,355 (+255 B, +1.3%)
  Mini minimal (z.string()):           2,707 -> 2,705  (-2 B, identical)
  Mini rich (object schema):           5,367 -> 5,365  (-2 B, identical)

Mini bundles are now byte-for-byte identical to main; classic overhead
is roughly halved versus the previous design (~430 B -> ~212 B gz).

All 3,743 tests still pass; heap/construction numbers unchanged.

* refactor(v4): drop layer indirection from lazy-bind helper

Install lazy method getters directly on each concrete schema's
`_.prototype` instead of inserting a library-owned layer between
`_.prototype` and its parent.

The layer was guarding `Object.keys(proto)` from seeing our methods,
but the existing copy-loop in `core.$constructor` already uses
`Object.keys` (enumerable own only), and our lazy getters are
non-enumerable. So the layer wasn't doing real work — just adding
prototype-chain depth and one `Object.setPrototypeOf` call per
constructor (the only V8-deopt-prone op in the helper).

Drops `_layerCache: WeakMap`, drops `Object.setPrototypeOf`, helper
shrinks from 45 to 30 lines. Behavior: `'optional' in
z.ZodString.prototype` is now `true` (was `false`) and
`Object.getOwnPropertyNames(z.ZodString.prototype)` now lists the
lazy method names — both arguably more intuitive since the methods
conceptually do live on the prototype.

Numbers (vs main, post-refactor):
  classic minimal bundle: +860 B raw / +175 B gz (was +212 gz)
  classic rich bundle:    +1,135 B raw / +221 B gz (was +255 gz)
  mini bundles:           byte-identical to main (unchanged)
  heap per instance:      same -40% as before
  construction:           same -25% as before

All 3,743 tests pass. User prototype extensions still work
(z.ZodType.prototype.x = ... copies to instances via the existing
copy-loop, and explicitly setting an enumerable value on the
prototype shadows the lazy getter as before).

* refactor(v4): type-check lazy method bodies against schema interfaces

The previous `_installLazyMethods` typed `methods` as
`Record<string, (this: any, ...args: any[]) => any>`, which gave
zero type safety on the inline method bodies — `this` was `any` and
arguments were unchecked, so any signature drift between the body
and the declared interface method silently slipped through.

Replace with a generic helper that derives the expected method
shapes from the instance's interface:

  type _LazyMethodsOf<T> = Partial<{
    [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends (...args: infer A) => infer R
      ? (this: T, ...args: A) => R
      : never;
  }>;

  function _installLazyMethods<T extends object>(
    inst: T,
    group: string,
    methods: _LazyMethodsOf<T>
  ): void

Each call site now infers `T` from `inst` (e.g. `ZodType` /
`_ZodString` / `ZodNumber` / `ZodArray` / `ZodObject`), and the
inline method bodies are checked against the interface declarations.
Adding/removing/renaming an arg in a body without updating the
interface (or vice versa) is now a compile error pointing at both
sites.

The only body that needed adjustment is `meta()`, which is
overloaded — the mapped type picks up the last overload, so we
return `any` from the body to satisfy both the no-arg and 1-arg
cases at runtime.

All 3,743 tests pass; same 13 pre-existing tsc errors as `main`.

* refactor(v4): drop redundant `: any` annotations from lazy method bodies

With the previous commit's strict typing on `_installLazyMethods`,
parameters in the inline method bodies receive their types via
contextual inference from the schema interfaces — explicit `: any`
annotations on every arg were leftover noise from before. Strip them.

Two methods need to keep variadic `any[]` because they intentionally
diverge from the picked overload's static signature at runtime:

- `meta(...args: any[]): any` — runtime branches on `args.length`
  to handle both `meta()` and `meta(data)` overloads, but the
  picked overload is `meta(data: GlobalMeta) => this`, which would
  type-narrow `args.length === 0` to "never true".
- `catchall(catchall)` — needs `catchall as any` on the spread
  because `SomeType` isn't structurally compatible with the strict
  `$ZodType` shape `clone` expects.

Everything else (~50 method bodies) loses its annotations and reads
as `optional() { ... }`, `min(value, params) { ... }`, etc. with full
contextual type-checking from the interface declarations.

query: Why do schema methods live on the prototype rather than as own properties on each instance, and what got measurably worse as a result?
text:
Add properties checks for instanceof schemas (#5912) Add properties checks for instanceof schemas (#5912)

* Add properties checks for instanceof schemas

* Revert "Add properties checks for instanceof schemas"

Replaced by a plain z.properties(shape) helper that returns an array of
ordinary $ZodCheckProperty checks. The dedicated $ZodCheckProperties check
type had no case in core/compile.ts, so any schema using it dropped off the
AOT fast path, and SupportedCheck there is a hand-listed union so nothing
caught the omission.

* Add z.properties() for checking several properties at once

Returns an array of ordinary $ZodCheckProperty checks to spread into the
existing variadic .check(), so there is no new check type, no new constructor,
and no per-schema-type method. Each check carries `when`, which opts it out of
the run loop's aborted-issue gate, so a parse reports every property that failed
rather than only the first.

* fix(v4): drop the always-run gate from z.properties

`when` opts a check past the *implicit* abort gate, not just the sibling-property
one. `runChecks` skips a `when`-carrying check only on `util.explicitlyAborted`, but
`z.object` / `z.record` / `z.array` push their type-mismatch issues with no `continue`
field, so the property checks ran against a value the base schema had already
rejected — and `$ZodCheckProperty` indexes `payload.value` unguarded.

    const obj = z.object({ a: z.string() }).check(...z.properties({ a: z.literal("x") }));
    obj.safeParse(null); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'a')
    obj.safeParse(5);    // invalid_type [] plus a spurious invalid_value ["a"]

A throwing `safeParse` is not a trade worth making for aggregated issue paths, so the
checks are now plain: `z.properties(shape)` is exactly the array of `z.property()`
calls it looks like, and behaves identically to writing them out. That also puts the
schema back on the compiled fast path, since `compile.ts` rejects any check carrying a
non-defaulted `when`.

The z.instanceof tests missed this because `_instanceof` aborts explicitly. The object
cases now cover null, undefined and a primitive.

* test(v4): pin where z.properties is looser than the longhand

Every element is typed over the whole shape, and `$ZodCheckInternals.check()` is a
method, so TypeScript compares it bivariantly and accepts a check type that is a
subtype of the target. Naming a key the target lacks compiles as a result, and fails
at parse time instead — where the equivalent chain of `z.property()` calls rejects it
outright.

Typing each element over only its own key restores the diagnostic and breaks every
valid call, because a union argument has to satisfy the target on its own. Pinning the
gap so it reads as a known trade rather than an accident.

query: Why is $ZodCatch marked optin === 'optional' unconditionally, and what regression did that restore?
text:
fix(v4): restore catch handling for absent object keys (#5937) (#5939) fix(v4): restore catch handling for absent object keys (#5937) (#5939)

`z.X.catch(...)` previously deferred its `optin` to the inner schema, so
when v4.4.0 tightened object parsing to reject absent keys whose schema
isn't `optin === "optional"`, fields like `z.preprocess(...).catch([])`
started failing on `{}` even though the catch handler should fire.

This restores the v4.3.x behavior by marking `$ZodCatch` as
`optin === "optional"` unconditionally. Catch always handles a missing
input gracefully (its handler runs with `undefined` and produces the
catch value), so it's correct to advertise that to `$ZodObject`.

To keep the existing `optional` semantics where an outer `.optional()`
short-circuits to `undefined` instead of surfacing the catch value, we
add an internal `caught` flag on `ParsePayload`. `$ZodCatch` sets it
unconditionally whenever `catchValue` fires; `handleOptionalResult`
reads it (alongside the existing `issues.length` check) to override the
result with `undefined` when the original input was `undefined`.

Hot path impact: the `caught` check lives in `handleOptionalResult`,
which only runs in `$ZodOptional`'s `optin === "optional"` branch.
Plain `z.string().optional()` parsing is unchanged (~3.3 ns / ~6.6 ns
present/undefined). The one regression is `.catch().optional()` parsing
`undefined`, which goes from ~37 ns to ~200 ns because `$ZodOptional`
no longer skips running the inner catch — that work is now necessary
for correctness.

query: Why is $ZodCatch marked optin === 'optional' unconditionally, and what regression did that restore?
text:
fix(v4): generalize optin/fallback to transform; restore preprocess on absent keys (#5941) fix(v4): generalize optin/fallback to transform; restore preprocess on absent keys (#5941)

* fix(v4): propagate fallback flag through pipe boundaries

`$ZodCatch` sets a payload flag when its `catchValue` substitutes so an
outer `$ZodOptional` can clobber the recovery value with `undefined`
(per #5939). But `handlePipeResult` was building a fresh payload for the
right side of the pipe without copying the flag, so any chain like
`catch().transform()...optional()` lost it — `optional` couldn't tell
the inner had recovered, and surfaced the catch value instead of
clobbering.

Propagate the flag through pipe handoffs, alongside `value`/`issues`.
Also rename `caught` to `fallback`: a slightly broader name that
describes the consumer contract ("override me if you have a better
value when input was undefined") rather than the producer ("catch fired
me"). Internal-only; no public API surface.

* fix(v4): restore preprocess handling for absent object keys

`z.object({ a: z.preprocess(fn, T) }).parse({})` worked in 4.3 (the fn
ran with `undefined`, produced a value, the inner schema validated it)
but started failing on absent keys after #5661 tightened the object
parser. Users commonly use preprocess to inject pre-parse defaults for
fields that may be missing — that pattern broke silently in 4.4.

Restore by marking $ZodPreprocess as `optin === "optional"`, telling
`$ZodObject` that absent keys are legal here. The fn then runs with
`undefined` exactly as it did in 4.3.

To preserve the long-stable behavior of `preprocess(fn, T).optional()
.parse(undefined)` returning `undefined` (true in both 4.3 and 4.4 for
multi-year compatibility), have `$ZodTransform` set the `fallback`
payload flag on every invocation. `$ZodOptional` already clobbers a
result with `fallback === true` when its input was `undefined`, so the
outer optional keeps short-circuiting to `undefined` even though the
transform now runs underneath.

  z.object({ a: z.preprocess(v => v ?? "X", z.string()) }).parse({})
  // 4.3:  { a: "X" }
  // 4.4:  FAIL  (regression)
  // now:  { a: "X" }

  z.preprocess(v => v ?? "X", z.string()).optional().parse(undefined)
  // 4.3 + 4.4:  undefined
  // now:        undefined  (preserved)

Drops the `optin` defer-to-inner from #5929, but the same outcome
holds: when inner is `.optional()`, preprocess still accepts absent
keys (`optin === "optional"` either way).

* fix(v4): generalize optin=optional from preprocess to transform

Promotes the "user-written input handler accepts absence" signal from
$ZodPreprocess to $ZodTransform. Any schema with a transform fn at its
input boundary (preprocess, standalone z.transform) now declares
optin="optional" at runtime.

Effects:
- preprocess inherits optin="optional" via pipe.optin = transform.optin
  (same outcome as the previous commit's explicit override; preprocess
  loses both its optin and optout overrides since pipe already does the
  optout defer)
- standalone z.transform(fn) now accepts absent object keys
- z.string().transform(fn): unchanged (pipe.optin = string.optin =
  undefined; transform on the OUT side doesn't drive optin)
- z.unknown().transform(fn).pipe(A): unchanged (pipe.optin = unknown.
  optin = undefined)

The static type stays unchanged — transform's interface doesn't
declare optin, so this only sets the runtime value, mirroring the
catch pattern. Captures the "flexible inputs, strict outputs" design
principle: schemas with a user-written escape hatch (catch's recovery,
transform's fn) accept undefined at runtime even when the static type
declares the input as required.

After this, $ZodPreprocess is a near-empty marker subtype — the
constructor body is just $ZodPipe.init(inst, def), kept for type
narrowing and traits identity.

* docs(wiki): add internal reference for v4 optionality semantics

Captures the current state of optin/optout/fallback, who sets each,
who reads each, the static/runtime divergence pattern, and walked-
through cases for the gnarly interactions (catch+optional, default
vs catch vs preprocess vs transform under optional, etc.).

Also documents the "flexible inputs, strict outputs" design principle
that motivates the runtime/static optin divergence on $ZodCatch and
$ZodTransform: schemas with a user-written escape hatch accept
undefined at runtime while keeping their declared input type strict.

Internal-only doc; not published.

* docs(wiki): explain why unknown.transform.pipe stays strict

Adds the explicit contrast between z.preprocess(fn, T) (= pipe(transform,
T), accepts absent) and z.unknown().transform(fn).pipe(T) (= pipe(pipe(
unknown, transform), T), rejects absent). The two look structurally
similar but only the leading position drives optin, and z.unknown()
isn't input-optional.

Also drops the stale "prototype only" caveat from the standalone
z.transform(fn) walkthrough — the runtime optin=optional move from
preprocess to transform is now a real part of this branch, not a
prototype.

query: Why is $ZodCatch marked optin === 'optional' unconditionally, and what regression did that restore?
text:
fix(v4): refine optin into a three-rung ladder, retire the fallback payload flag (#6419) fix(v4): refine optin into a three-rung ladder, retire the fallback payload flag (#6419)

`optin` was overloaded across two readers asking different questions. $ZodObject/$ZodTuple asked "may this slot be absent?"; $ZodOptional asked "should I invoke you on undefined and trust the result?". $ZodTransform and $ZodCatch set optin="optional" to satisfy the first, which made the second draw the wrong conclusion — and payload.fallback existed only to undo it. That undo was itself unsound: it marked every transform invocation, so a .default() between the transform and an outer .optional() had its value discarded.

Refine the value instead of adding a sibling:

  undefined    required
  "optional"   the container may omit it; nothing is supplied
  "defaulted"  the container may omit it AND this schema substitutes

"May the slot be absent?" becomes `!== undefined`. $ZodOptional asks the stronger question and tests `=== "defaulted"`, running the inner only when something down there actually answers the absence. payload.fallback is removed entirely.

A restoration rather than an invention: `_zod.optionality` carried these same three values until #4405 split the axis into optin/optout and collapsed the ladder as collateral, pre-4.0.0.

BREAKING (internals): `optin` is now "defaulted" rather than "optional" for default/prefault. Introspection that tests `optin === "optional"` should test `optin !== undefined`. z.input/z.output inference is unaffected.

Closes #6321. Supersedes #6329.

query: Why do the ZodISODateTime / ZodISODate class definitions live in classic/schemas.ts rather than in classic/iso.ts?
text:
fix(v4): break circular import between classic schemas and iso (#5275) (#5926) fix(v4): break circular import between classic schemas and iso (#5275) (#5926)

* fix(v4): break circular import between classic schemas and iso (#5275)

`packages/zod/src/v4/classic/schemas.ts` imported `./iso.js` to forward
deprecated `ZodString.{datetime,date,time,duration}` proxies, while
`./iso.js` imported back from `./schemas.js` to extend `ZodStringFormat`.
Rollup (and other bundlers) reported this two-way cycle.

Move the `ZodISODateTime/Date/Time/Duration` class definitions into
`schemas.ts` next to their `ZodStringFormat` base, and call the
underlying `core._iso*` builders directly from the deprecated proxies.
`iso.ts` becomes a thin namespace facade that re-exports the classes
from `schemas.ts` and exposes the `z.iso.{datetime,date,time,duration}`
builder functions.

Public API is unchanged - `z.iso.datetime()`, `z.iso.ZodISODateTime`,
top-level `ZodISODateTime`, and `z.string().datetime()` all behave as
before. The cycle is gone in both directions.

Adds two regression tests:

- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/no-circular-imports.test.ts` - fast
  static-analysis check over the classic source tree (DFS on the import
  graph); fails on any future cycle.
- `packages/treeshake/tests/no-circular-imports.test.ts` - bundles three
  zod entries via rollup's programmatic API (concurrently) and asserts
  no `CIRCULAR_DEPENDENCY` warning involves zod sources. Mirrors the
  exact rollup pass that originally surfaced the issue.

* test(treeshake): bump testTimeout to 180s for CI cold-start

The 3 concurrent rollup builds in no-circular-imports.test.ts run ~35s
locally on Windows but exceed the 60s default on Linux CI cold-start
(rollup is CPU-bound on TS parsing; concurrency doesn't help much).
Bump to 180s so the regression test for #5275 doesn't time out.

query: Why do the ZodISODateTime / ZodISODate class definitions live in classic/schemas.ts rather than in classic/iso.ts?
text:
fix: strip redundant id from $defs entries in toJSONSchema (#5759) fix: strip redundant id from $defs entries in toJSONSchema (#5759)

* fix: strip id from $defs entries in toJSONSchema

Fixes #5731

When a schema is annotated with .meta({ id: "Name" }), the id is used
as the key in $defs so that other schemas can reference it. However,
the id was also included verbatim in the definition body, producing
redundant (and invalid) output like:

  "$defs": {
    "Inner": {
      "id": "Inner",   ← redundant
      "type": "string"
    }
  }

In extractToDef(), after copying the schema into seen.def, delete id
from the definition body when it matches the defId — the id is already
encoded as the $defs key name.

* refactor: move id strip to finalize() and also strip from root

The `id` in `.meta()` is a Zod-specific registration tag that controls
$defs extraction — it is not user-facing JSON Schema metadata. Strip it
from the output body in two places:

1. From each $defs entry where it equals the defId (already covered).
2. From the root schema where it equals the user-set metadata id.

Move the strip to finalize() so that the override callback still observes
`jsonSchema.id` on extracted definitions — preserves backward-compat for
userland override handlers that read it.

Adds explicit tests for:
- $defs strip (draft-2020-12)
- definitions strip (draft-04, where `id` is a reserved keyword)
- root strip
- override-callback observability

query: Why do the ZodISODateTime / ZodISODate class definitions live in classic/schemas.ts rather than in classic/iso.ts?
text:
feat(v4): add z.creditCard() string format (#5931) feat(v4): add z.creditCard() string format (#5931)

Adds `z.creditCard()` to Zod and Zod Mini. Closes #4039.

Validation is shape plus [Luhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luhn_algorithm): 12–19 digits, optionally separated by single spaces or single hyphens, with a valid checksum. The issuer is not identified.

That last part is the main change from the original version of this PR, which ran an allowlist of seven issuer regexes between the shape check and the checksum. An allowlist rejects any Luhn-valid card from a scheme it doesn't know, and this one turned away Mir, Elo, Hipercard, Troy, Verve, Dankort, RuPay, Maestro's 5018 range, UATP, and Discover's own 644–649 range — 11 of 22 real in-use BIN ranges. Branding needs a BIN table with its own update cadence, so it belongs with the payment processor rather than in Zod.

The deprecated `z.string().creditCard()` chainable is gone for the same reason it was never a good idea: assigning it on `ZodString` pins the validator into every bundle that touches `z.string()`. As a standalone format it tree-shakes out — a user who never calls `z.creditCard()` pays 37 bytes for the locale label and nothing else.

One more fix worth calling out: the outer shape regex never bounded the total digit count. Its grouped alternatives accepted 10 to 28 digits, and the issuer allowlist was the only thing catching that, so dropping the allowlist would have made the bug live. It is now a single pattern that means what it says.

Thanks to @dokson for the implementation and for the Mastercard regex precedence fix, and to @ysknsid25, who filed #4037 for this same feature the day the issue went up and carried it for 17 months. The Luhn routine is adapted from valibot (MIT, attributed at the call site).

query: Was rejecting whitespace in z.base64() ever implemented in this repository? If so, what happened to it?
text:
fix(v4): reject whitespace in z.base64() to close atob bypass fix(v4): reject whitespace in z.base64() to close atob bypass

atob() strips ASCII whitespace before validating, which let strings like
"123 " sneak past the length-mod-4 short-circuit in isValidBase64. Reject
whitespace explicitly before the length check so the runtime matches the
strict regex we already advertise via bag.patterns / contentEncoding.

Refs #5865.

query: In the JSON Schema tuple processor, why is minItems derived from an optin/optout walk rather than from prefixItems.length?
text:
fix(json-schema): resolve tuple minItems past transform and catch in input mode (#6418) fix(json-schema): resolve tuple minItems past transform and catch in input mode (#6418)

* fix(json-schema): resolve tuple minItems past transform and catch in input mode

#6133 routed objectProcessor's `required` list through `inputOptin` so an input
JSON Schema describes the declared input type rather than the runtime `optin`
flag. tupleProcessor's `minItems` tail scan was left reading the runtime flag,
so the same divergence stayed live for tuples:

  z.toJSONSchema(z.tuple([z.string(), z.preprocess(v => v, z.string())]), { io: "input" })
  // minItems: 1, but z.input<> is [string, string] and .safeParse(["a"]) rejects

That output matched neither the declared type nor the parser. The object
equivalent already emitted required: ["a", "b"].

Route the input-mode scan through the same helper. Output mode still reads
`optout` directly — the divergence is input-side only. A trailing `.default()`
or `.optional()` still shortens `minItems`, since those declare optional input
statically; resolution passes through the wrapper, so a catch over an optional
inner shortens too.

No existing snapshot changes: the affected cases had no coverage, which is why
this survived. Adds one.

* docs: update the TL;DR row now that both emitters resolve statically

The consumer table still said tupleProcessor reads the runtime value, which
this PR makes false.

query: In the JSON Schema tuple processor, why is minItems derived from an optin/optout walk rather than from prefixItems.length?
text:
fix(toJSONSchema): constrain closed tuple length (#6194) fix(toJSONSchema): constrain closed tuple length (#6194)

`tupleProcessor` never emitted length bounds for a closed tuple, so the generated schema accepted arrays `.parse()` rejects. `$ZodTuple` bounds a rest-less tuple by `getTupleOptStart(items, "optin" | "optout")` below and `items.length` above; the generator emitted neither for the draft targets.

Each target now gets the tail keyword it actually defines — `additionalItems: false` for draft-04/draft-07, `items: false` for draft-2020-12 (which removed `additionalItems`), and nothing for openapi-3.0, whose Schema Object has no equivalent and whose `items` must be a single schema. `minItems`/`maxItems` are supported by all four and emitted in all four, with `minItems` derived from the same optin/optout walk the parser uses, so it tracks `ctx.io`.

That also repairs two openapi-3.0 defects the report did not cover, both of which made the emitted schema stricter than `.parse()`:

- `minItems` was `prefixItems.length`, ignoring an optional or defaulted tail, so `z.tuple([z.string(), z.number().optional()])` emitted `minItems: 2` while `.safeParse(["a"])` succeeds.
- `json.items = { anyOf: prefixItems }` aliases the array and `.push(rest)` grows it, so `minItems` read `items.length + 1`. `z.tuple([z.string(), z.number()]).rest(z.boolean())` emitted `minItems: 3`, rejecting the valid `["a", 1]`. Reading `def.items` fixes the count; the aliasing itself remains and is worth a follow-up.

The six updated snapshots were each checked against the runtime accept set. `tuple with rest openapi-3.0` moving from `minItems: 3` to `2` is the aliasing fix, not a regression.

fix(v4): resolve stack overflow in toJSONSchema for recursive lazy with describe (#5797) fix(v4): resolve stack overflow in toJSONSchema for recursive lazy with describe (#5797)

* fix(v4): resolve stack overflow in toJSONSchema for recursive lazy with describe

When .describe() or .meta() is called on a recursive z.lazy() schema,
the clone re-evaluates the getter on each recursion level, producing
unbounded new schema objects. Walk up to the root lazy to reuse its
cached innerType instead.

Fixes #5777.

* fix(v4): cache lazy innerType on def so clones share identity

Move the recursion fix from the JSON-schema processor into the $ZodLazy
constructor. Caching the resolved inner type on the shared `def` means
all clones of a lazy (via .describe(), .meta(), etc.) resolve to the
same inner instance, so cycle detection works for any consumer — not
just toJSONSchema — and parsing no longer rebuilds a fresh subtree on
every access through a clone.
